name: Freya Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the wet end of a corrugator that glues wavy paper between flat sheets to make cardboard board. I watch the steam, glue and reels, then splice fresh paper without stopping the line. Fifteen years and a vocational certificate have earned me a better-than-usual operator wage, though summer heat can still beat me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who is at home, and how do you use new technology?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Sam is a self-employed plumber with one apprentice, and our school-age children Hannah and Joseph are thirteen and ten. We have a mortgage, about a year saved and plenty of other factories nearby. I have never used AI tools; I ask a person before trusting a new panel and see our friends at church on Sundays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the wet-end crew that an AI quiet spell sounds about right. The glue pot still needs someone who can smell a weak mix before a whole reel is wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My corrugator shifts and higher operator wage would stay familiar. Sam’s plumbing business brings work in unevenly, but we have about a year of expenses saved and plenty of other plants nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the six-to-two shift and check the paper splice by hand. From full paid months I would send a fresh amount to our savings account, and I would ask Sam for a proper bathroom quote before we decide to redo it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel calm about the job, though the summer heat still drains me. A quiet machine is a good machine only if the board comes out square.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you ever used AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I can work the corrugator screen, but I have never used an AI tool and do not want one telling me about glue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why get a bathroom quote now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam can do the plumbing, but the tile and fittings still cost money. We would only go ahead if the mortgage payment and year of savings remain comfortable.

I would still check **glue and splices** by hand.
think: My **higher factory wage** stays familiar in the plateau.
Sam’s **uneven plumbing work** is buffered by roughly a year saved.
do: Keep **six-to-two corrugator shifts** and inspect paper splices.
Add fresh **full-month wages** to our savings account.
Ask for a **bathroom quote** before deciding on fittings.
feel: **Calm** about work, despite tiring summer heat.
S0.quote: A quiet machine is a good machine only if the board comes out square.
fieldNote: Freya trusts **felt machine knowledge** from years on the wet end.
Her **year-long reserve** and strong pay let her discuss a bathroom, while the decision still depends on actual costs.

steps.text: Keep corrugator shifts and check paper splices by hand
Add fresh full-month wages to household savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the owners can modernise, but they should keep experienced hands on the line and pay apprentices to learn. A splicer video is not a staffing plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office might change first, then a proven automatic splicer could remove half my wet-end hours. Sam’s plumbing bookings are uneven, so his earnings would not replace my factory wage if the roster thinned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the next two rosters and keep my present shifts. If my own paid hours fall, we would postpone the bathroom and I would apply for a posted reachable corrugator job only where the wage covers our bills; I would ask for safe paid instruction on any new splicer before touching it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a cut to hours. I can manage a new machine if someone shows me properly, but I will not guess beside live paper reels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course on your own time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, evenings are for the children and I have never used AI tools. If the plant offers a paid, guarded practice slot with a qualified operator, I would consider it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who could help with childcare if a shift changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My church neighbours could sometimes help with pickup, but I would ask them first. I cannot build a permanent rota on a favour.

say: I would ask owners for a **real staffing plan** before automatic splicers.
I would defend **paid apprenticeships** for experienced crews.
think: A proven splicer could cut **my wet-end hours**.
Sam’s **variable plumbing bookings** cannot replace my higher factory wage alone.
do: Keep **current shifts** and request two written rosters.
Postpone the **bathroom** after actual paid-hour cuts.
Apply for **posted reachable corrugator work** only at bill-covering pay after cuts.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible reduction to her own hours.
S1.quote: I can manage a new machine if someone shows me properly, but I will not guess beside live paper reels.
fieldNote: Her **resistance to AI** still allows supervised mechanical instruction on a safe stopped line.
The course is a **request**, and the bathroom delay and outside application follow real hour cuts and adequate postings.

steps.text: Keep corrugator shifts and request next two written rosters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell church friends that thinking AGI might arrive by 2028, while capable hands-on robots come around 2031. The robots, when they can splice reels and reach under sinks, are what threaten our two trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my corrugator hours to end around 2031, and Sam may lose plumbing jobs then too. A year saved helps, but two wages at risk and a mortgage would keep me awake at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would cancel the planned bathroom and summer trip and ask the plant for staffing dates. If my shifts end, I would apply for posted reachable factory work only if the wage covers our bills; if no adequate post exists, I would ask our church group about temporary childcare and the lender about payment terms before we miss the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed because I expect a large household income loss. I can ask for help, but I cannot make another factory hire me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you help Sam with bookings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If his plumbing customers still call, I would handle the phone and his paper diary after my shift ends. That would support his business, but I would not count it as a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you use the reserve for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not pay for a course without a posted reachable job at a usable wage and an offered safe place. The mortgage has first claim on that money.

say: I would separate **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 physical robots.
I would name **both trades** as exposed when capable robots arrive.
think: I expect **most corrugator hours** and some plumbing work to go.
One **year saved** cannot replace two wages indefinitely.
do: Cancel **bathroom and trip** and request staffing dates.
Apply after **lost shifts** only for posted reachable bill-covering work.
Ask **church and lender** for temporary help if no adequate job appears.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major income loss and sleepless mortgage worry.
S2.quote: I can ask for help, but I cannot make another factory hire me.
fieldNote: Her **hands-on risk** rises with capable robots around 2031, after earlier thinking AGI.
Helping Sam’s diary is **unpaid family support**; local employment and payment relief depend on actual postings and approval.

steps.text: Cancel bathroom and summer trip and request staffing dates
Apply after lost shifts for posted reachable bill-covering factory work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the town meeting that thinking AGI in 2031 and capable factory robots around 2034 give us five years. The council should help employers advertise real apprenticeships and local jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At forty-eight I will still need the mortgage wage, even if Hannah and Joseph are older. I might waste the first year hoping the corrugator stays the same, so Sam and I would put a monthly figure on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the wet-end shift and put a fresh part of each full wage month against mortgage principal. If the plant offers a funded, paid-time course on safe reel maintenance with an actual supervised place, and a posted reachable maintenance vacancy pays our bills, I would enrol and apply after qualifying; if no place opens, I would search posted nearby operator roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious, but the extra years give me time to look at a real offer. I would rather change a reel beside a fitter than pretend a video trained me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe reel practice involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The corrugator would be isolated, and a qualified fitter would show me how to adjust tension without a live web pulling my hands. I would need an offered paid practice slot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Joseph join Sam’s business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if my son Joseph wants to and a proper paid plumbing apprenticeship is available when he is old enough. Sam and I would talk with him before making plans for his life.

say: I would ask for **real local apprenticeships** before 2034 robots.
I would separate **2031 planning AI** from later physical change.
think: The **mortgage wage** will still matter every month when I turn forty-eight.
A **fridge figure** may keep me from postponing every decision.
do: Keep **wet-end shifts** and pay extra mortgage principal from fresh wages.
Enrol in **funded paid reel training** only with safe place and adequate posted role.
Apply after **qualification** for that reachable maintenance vacancy.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to test real offers.
S3.quote: I would rather change a reel beside a fitter than pretend a video trained me.
fieldNote: She accepts **practical maintenance learning** only if the employer funds paid safe instruction.
The later **application** follows qualification and requires a posted reachable job at bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Pay extra mortgage principal from fresh full-month wages

Apply after qualification for posted reachable bill-covering maintenance job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell church friends that thinking AGI in 2036 and capable factory robots around 2039 leave time to prepare. We should ask the plant and local firms for real dates, not make the children live under rumours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be fifty-three when thinking systems arrive and fifty-six when robots may splice reels. The children will be adults, but I cannot assume our mortgage is gone or Sam’s customers still call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the corrugator shifts and pay extra mortgage principal from fresh wages when bills permit. In the first year after 2036, if I am still on the line, I would compare written rosters with posted nearby work; after an actual sustained cut, I would apply only for safe reachable work paying our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about the distant robots while our present income is secure. A decade is useful, but it is not a promise of work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire before 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check our mortgage and retirement figures with Sam before deciding. I do not know our income then, so I cannot promise an exit from factory work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Hannah and Joseph to learn a trade only if it has a real paid place and they want it. Sunday dinner is for hearing their plans, not handing them mine.

I would keep **2036 AI** separate from later splicing machines.
think: Our **mortgage and plumbing bookings** remain uncertain years ahead.
I cannot assume **retirement income** or a factory job at fifty-six.

Check **post-2036 rosters** only if still employed.
Apply after **sustained cuts** for posted reachable safe bill-covering work.
feel: **Uneasy** about distant change while today’s income is secure.
S4.quote: A decade is useful, but it is not a promise of work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Which picture worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could take corrugator shifts and plumbing bookings before we can change course. Written staffing dates, paid safe training and real posted jobs at bill-covering pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether people will still need one another when the wet end is quiet. I want Hannah and Joseph to know that work has a place at our table.

headlineQuote: I want Hannah and Joseph to know that work has a place at our table.
portrait: **Freya**, 43, runs a corrugator’s wet end with a vocational certificate and fifteen years of practical paper-splicing experience.
Her **plumber husband**, two school-age children, mortgage, high factory pay and year-long reserve give stability despite uneven plumbing bookings.
She has **never used AI**, leans on family and church, and accepts new machine work only through offered safe paid instruction.
Fast robots threaten **both trades**, while slower arrival permits conditional maintenance training and fresh-wage mortgage payments.
biggestWorry: **Fast hands-on robots** could cut both corrugator work and plumbing bookings around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: Written **staffing dates**, offered paid safe practice and posted reachable jobs paying household bills would help.
